WhatItMeans: People take it as a given that the Bible lists seven deadly sins — pride, greed, lust, envy, gluttony, wrath and sloth — a fixed set, named and counted in Scripture.
WhatTheBibleSays: Each of those vices is warned against in Scripture, but the set of seven is not from the Bible at all — it is a church list, shaped by monks and popes centuries after the apostles. The verse people usually mean is Proverbs 6:16-19: "These six things doth the LORD hate: yea, seven are an abomination unto him" — but that list is a proud look, a lying tongue, hands that shed innocent blood, a heart that devises wicked imaginations, feet swift in running to mischief, a false witness, and one who sows discord. Only pride appears on both lists. My position is that the seven deadly sins are a useful catalogue of human failure, but they are the church's list, not the Bible's, and the Bible's own seven are mostly outward acts — lying, murder, perjury, sowing division — while the church's seven are mostly inward appetites.
Origin: The list began as eight "evil thoughts" of the desert monk Evagrius Ponticus (c. 346-399), was carried west by John Cassian (c. 360-435) in The Institutes, and was reshaped into seven by Pope Gregory the Great in his Moralia in Job (c. 590): vainglory folded into pride, sadness into acedia (sloth), envy added, pride set as the root. Thomas Aquinas later expounded Gregory's list as the "capital sins" in the Summa Theologica (1265-1274), and the Catechism of the Catholic Church names them in paragraph 1866.
Sources: Evagrius Ponticus; John Cassian, The Institutes; Pope Gregory the Great, Moralia in Job (c. 590); on-site KJV text of Proverbs 6:16-19 and Galatians 5:19-21
